Upon attaining the reality within this secret wheel through the secret wisdom initiation,
one becomes a knower of the secret, a knower of the reality of yoga, and a knower of the reality of the union of the three vehicles.

He is one who, according to the principles of the Tantra, knows the divisions of the vidyās, heart-mantras, and mudrās, as well as the three types of samādhi and the common and extraordinary accomplishments.

Whether established in the vows of the pledge or intensely devoted to the yoga of wisdom, one who knows the application of mantra and tantra is fit for accomplishing the welfare of sentient beings. //5//

Even one endowed with renunciation, fortitude, and so forth, if lacking the aforementioned qualities, is not fit for the welfare of sentient beings; for these [other] virtues exist only when those [qualities] are present.
Compassionate, firm in his vows, a practitioner of recitation, endowed with faith, and knowing the profound reality,
one who has performed the preliminary service while established in his own mandala-cakra should draw the mandala.
In a certain place agreeable to the mind, smeared with excellent sandalwood and the like, strewn with fragrant flowers, and having sat down there early in the morning; ||8||
For the sake of purifying the gateways to liberation, one should meditate on the syllable *maṃ*, blazing with light, within the moon at the heart;
then, for the purpose of increasing virtue, one should perform the teaching and other such activities. (9)
Standing before the Buddhas arisen in all directions and throughout the three times,
one should perform worship according to the ritual procedure by means of forms and other offerings arising from the light of the heart.
Whatever evil deeds I have committed throughout the three times, arising solely from my own false conceptualizations—just like dreams within dreams—I confess them all three times over. (11)
Having rejoiced in all the merit—whether of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, their true sons, the Noble Ones, or others—without exception, I dedicate it toward supreme enlightenment. 12.
I entreat all the Buddhas, who bestow consolation upon all, to let this faultless [teaching], which abides in the expanse of space, shine throughout the entire world. (13)

I go for refuge to the perfectly awakened ones, who possess entirely pure intentions, who experience the bliss of their own inner self, and who bestow the fruits of the welfare of both themselves and others. (14)

I go for refuge to the true, inconceivable Sanctuary, which is the source of all excellence, consisting of the scriptures and realizations of the sublime Dharma of all sentient beings without exception. (15)
I have gone for refuge to the assembly that has attained irreversible confidence, endowed with the fruits such as the outflow, and born from the secret initiation. (16)

Therefore, I now take refuge with the true mind that is the essence of all Buddhas in the excellent path of the Son of the Lord of Munis, which consists of conduct leading to infinite and supreme enlightenment. (17)
Having utterly destroyed all obscurations, I have established myself in the abode of the nectar of infinite knowledge;
for the sake of awakening those with deluded views, I direct my entire mind toward enlightenment. (18)
Buddhahood arises from the thought of awakening because the cause is unattached;
since it is a reality to be personally realized, I am indeed of the nature of the wisdom of emptiness. (19)
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness.
Or else, [one should visualize] the syllable HŪṂ, or the Uṣṇīṣa,
or indeed Śāśvata and the others.
For the sake of protection, one situated within the wheel of wrath should meditate, crushing all obstacles.
Then one should meditate upon the dharmadhātu as a white triangle situated upright, possessing various colors that revolve through the directions, located within the space-lotus-vajra. 21.
Therein, [the mandala] arises from the wheel of the syllable *Bhrūṃ*, originating from the eternal one together with the Vidyā;
it pervades the sky with a radiating flood of Buddhas and is endowed with the square and other [geometric forms]. (22)
One should visualize a peaked pavilion resting upon a seat of a universal lotus and deities, pervaded by the moon and sun, and adorned with all kinds of excellent jewels distributed throughout. (23)
Having visualized that mind as the moon of gnosis upon the central moon-seat, endowed with the characteristics of vowels and possessing the rays of the consonants beginning with *ka*. (24)

There, one should visualize a red vajra arising from the first heart-mantra, joined with that same first heart-mantra; having assumed the identity of that [vajra] for the purpose of manifesting the body of the Jina’s essence, one should oneself [become it]. (25)
His face has a body like crystal and the moon; his right side is blue and the other (left) is red;
he is magnificent with the excellence of all forms, adorned with the ornaments and garments of virtuous qualities. (26)
Embraced by the excellent Prajñā with two arms, he is firmly established in the vajra-paryaṅka posture;
his right hands hold a vajra and a sword, while his left hands hold an excellent jewel and a lotus. (27)
One should meditate upon oneself as Samantabhadra, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means, the glorious refuge of the world’s prosperity, and who radiates light in all directions. (28)
Having beheld that world as a vessel to be disciplined by great passion, one should cause the assembly of Victors to enter within oneself with the sound of supreme bliss. (29)

Having projected the nine goddesses, whose natures consist of the objects such as form and the like, along with their corresponding vidyās beginning with Locanā, one should cause them to enter within one's own vidyā.
Having fashioned within his own wife, who is like a *karkaṭī* gourd, a mandala arising from sexual union,
he should cause the entire world to enter therein for the sake of its consolation.
One should sprinkle [the disciple] with those who pervade the sky, who are like friends to the Buddhas, and who arise from the internal melting of one's own vajra;
this is for the sake of non-retrogression and for the attainment of the fruit of the knowledge of reality. 32.
Seeing that world thus comforted by seeds born of its own nature, one should relinquish all sentient beings, who are born from the mind-nature of the world. (33)

One should [visualize] the six [bodhisattvas] beginning with Kṣitigarbha, who arise from the nature of the eye and the other [senses], by means of these [syllables] together with their seeds in due order: kṣīṃ, jrāṃ, khāṃ, gāṃ, ṣkaṃ, and saṃ. ||34||

The six [deities] beginning with Rūpavajrā, who arise from the nature of the external and internal, are situated outside the seed-syllable *raṃ*, [emanated] by means of these syllables: *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, *hoḥ*, and *khaṃ*. (35)

Locanā and the other vidyās arise from the intrinsic nature of earth and the other elements; they are born from the reality of the self-nature of the world and phenomena through these [syllables]: lāṃ, māṃ, pāṃ, tāṃ. (36)
One should abandon the notions of the Buddhas as being eternal and so forth, as well as the notion that they arise from the intrinsic nature of the aggregates such as form;
one should relinquish all phenomena by means of the syllables *būṃ*, *āṃ*, *jrīṃ*, *khaṃ*, and *hūṃ*. (37)
"Oṃ Āḥ Hūṃ"—thus that mind, interwoven with the two syllables Bhāḥ and Svāḥ, is situated within the interior of the secret lotus for the sake of purifying the gentle outflow. (38)
And one should meditate on them as being set ablaze by the fire of passion, their two bodies liquefied,
and receiving excellent exhortations through the songs of the goddesses of the directions who appear as true friends.
(One who provides excellent exhortation should request [the teaching] with the song of the goddesses of the directions, appearing as a true friend. ||39||
O Vajra-mind, Lord of the world, protect me within the realm of sentient beings with your delightful passion for the sake of the great purpose;
desire me, O Father, greatest kinsman of all beings!
If you desire my life, O Mañjunātha! ||40||
O you of vajra-body, whose command-wheel is beloved by many beings, who perceive the welfare of the ultimate meaning of awakening and the purpose of the Buddhas—
through passion, please love me, who am the pledge of passion.
If you desire my life, O Mañjunātha! ||41||
O Vajravāc, you who are compassionate for the benefit of all and always engaged in performing deeds for the sake of the world—
O Samantabhadra, desire me for the practice of supreme bliss!
If you wish for me to live, O Mañjunātha! ||42||
O Vajrakāma, supreme of commitments, you who act for the great benefit of others, the ornament of the lineage of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, and who possess equal compassion;
desire me, a treasury of virtues who have become like many jewels.
If you wish for me to live, O Mañjunātha! ||43||

Out of regard for what must be established, seeing that fluidity as if it were a calamity, the meaning of one's own mantra may arise again through the perception of reality as being like an illusion. (44)
His face has a root [channel] shaped like saffron; he is blue on the left and white on the other side;
his appearance is adorned like that of a youth; he is uniquely beautiful with the bliss of wisdom. ||45||
Embraced by his excellent Prajñā with two arms, he holds his own Prajñā upon his lap;
his hands bear a radiant sword, an excellent arrow, a blue lotus, and a bow. ||46||

Having brought the three worlds to completion through the emanations of the surging flood of Buddhas, one should oneself become Mañjuvajra, arisen from the sign produced by one's own seed-syllable. (47)
From attachment to existence, existence becomes endless; attachment to tranquility brings about misfortune.
One who has cultivated association through illusion shall become identical with the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu).
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the dharmadhātu.
Having been brought to maturation by virtuous friends through the flow [of their teachings], one attains omniscience;
that empowerment of the eyes and so forth is intended as the *upasādhana*. (49)
Having filled the eyes and other sense organs with the syllables of Kṣitīśa, Kuliśa, Ākāśa, Lokeśa, Skambhi, and Bhadraka, one should carry forth the heroic power (pauruṣa).
The fulfillment of the world's purpose flows through the Dharmakāya, Sambhogakāya, and Nirmāṇakāya;
therefore, for the sake of accomplishment, there is the empowerment of the secrets of the mind and so forth. ||51||

Having meditated upon the Lords of Secrets—Citta and the others—seated within a vajra, lotus, and wheel, respectively, and arising from the syllables HŪṂ, ĀḤ, and OṂ located in the moon at one’s own heart, throat, and head; 52.

Having worshipped all the Vināyakas who pervade all directions and the three times with rays [issuing] from the flames produced by contact with the limbs of Prajñā, which are like clarified butter, and with the light-rays of Rūpavajrā and the others; ||53||
For those who have accomplished the perfection of their goals, one should accomplish the Mind-Vajra and the others located in the heart, throat, and head by means of that very empowerment. (54)
May the glorious holder of the mind-vajra, who is meditated upon as the indivisibility of the three vajras, grant me today the state of empowerment of the Mind-Vajrin. (55)
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are conceived as the indivisibility of the three vajras, grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra of Mind! (56)
Oṃ! I am of the nature of the vajra-mind of all Tathāgatas.
The glorious Dharma is indeed the path of speech, cultivated as the indivisibility of the three vajras.
May it grant me today the state of empowerment of the Vajra-Speech. (57)
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are meditated upon as the indivisible three vajras, grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra of Speech! (58)
Oṃ! I am of the nature of the speech-vajra of all Tathāgatas.
May the glorious Holder of the Body-Vajra, who is cultivated as the indivisibility of the three vajras, grant me today the state of empowerment as the Body-Vajra-holder. (59)
May the Buddhas residing in the ten directions, who are realized as the indivisibility of the three vajras, grant me today the state of empowerment, O Vajra-Body beings! (60)
"Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-body of all Tathāgatas. He spoke thus because they perform [the purification] for the sake of the purity of the sixteen recollections (*anusmṛti*).
The consecration of his mind and so forth was not mentioned, as it would have been an irrelevant statement. (61)

Having observed the characteristics of the three secrets, through union with the limbs of Māyā-prajñā, the Great Accomplishment (mahāsādhana) is intended for the sake of gentle, stainless, and complete purification.
Having exhorted the Protectors situated in the directions with the light from the heart of the Knowledge Being,
[he should consecrate] with the vidyās arising from that radiance and with the waters of nectar from the filled jars.

The glorious Lord, consecrated by himself and possessing the supreme crown of the Lord of the Family, should purify his own innate Wisdom through the [five] outflows and so forth, as well as the intermediate ones. (64)
One should place the individual atoms at the head, heart, navel, secret place, and the ends of the feet,
using the syllables OṂ HŪṂ SVĀHṚD (HRĪḤ), along with ĀḤ and HĀ, which embody the families beginning with Śāśvata.

Having filled the eight-petaled lotus with the five Buddhas—HŪṂ ĀḤ—and having thoroughly purified it, one who possesses the vajra of the syllable HŪṂ should cause the Buddhas to be impassioned by means of that [lotus]. (66)
Oṃ! I am of the nature of the Vajra of the passion of all Tathāgatas.
Having established within myself the maṇḍala of Buddhas, which pervades space through the light from the sword at the heart-moon, I take on the form of the true mind, resting upon a vajra-lotus. (67)

Having generated the wheel of the Jina there by means of its own seed-syllable and rendered it stable, one should emit it according to this procedure for the purification of one’s own knowledge of the world. (68)
Having exhorted the Lord Akṣobhya, the Victor who accomplishes the purpose through great hatred,
he emitted [the deity] Vajradhṛk, who possesses the luster of a sapphire.
The glorious one, having withdrawn into himself that which is white on the left, red on the other, and endowed with supreme primordial arms, should cause it to enter by means of all states of being.

One should likewise meditate upon the Lord Jinajik, who possesses the splendor of the first [moon], who effects the purpose of great delusion, and who is endowed with the true wheel and other [attributes], within the eastern lunar mandala.
"Ratnadhṛk"—thus [one should meditate on] Ratneśa, who has a golden luster and is endowed with noble jewels and so forth; the Lord has the face of a youth and is positioned to the right.
ĀROLI is Vāgīśa, the Lord who accomplishes the purpose of great passion;
he has the luster of a ruby, is seated upon a lotus, and has youthful faces at the back. (73)

One should meditate on Amogheśa, who bears wisdom, is born from the syllable *kha*, possesses a great mountain-like envy, accomplishes purposes, has the luster of beryl, and has the face of a youth; he holds a sword and other implements in the northern direction. (74)

All [the deities] should be meditated upon as wearing crowns of matted hair, joined with their respective consorts, adorned with all ornaments and fine garments, seated upon a lotus and solar mandala. (75)
Moharati is in the southeast; she bestows the purpose of birth through compassion and skillful means.
Locanā, whose nature is like that of Kāyeśvara, resides within her own lunar mandala. (76)
In the southwest is Māmakī, who delights in hatred; she bestows the desire for the vow of loving-kindness, and like Citteśa, she possesses zeal for her vow within the lunar mandala.
In the northwest is Rāgarati, who bestows joy, strength, and meditative concentration;
she is Vāgīśā, pure in her purpose, and is Pāṇḍarā upon the lunar disc. (78)
And Vajrarati, who accomplishes the gnosis of equanimity, is in the northeast;
she has the same nature as Ratneśa, and Tārā is beautiful upon the moon. (79)
A wheel, a divine red lotus, a yellow lotus, and the remaining [symbols] are taught as their respective insignia in sequence, according to their own lords. (80)

In the four corners beginning with the southeast, and on both sides of the eastern gate, there are Rūpā and the others with mirrors and so forth; and Kāyā and the others, according to the three principles (tattvas). 81.

At the eastern gate is Yamāntaka, resplendent with the form of Citteśa, seated upon a wrathful throne; he is the destroyer of the great obstacles, through the destruction of the aggregates and the objects of knowledge. 82.
He is the fierce lord of the body, undefeated at the gate of speech;
he is the ender of passion and the destroyer of desire through the abandonment of afflictions regarding the vision of his own self. ||83||
The destroyer of the flood of birth and death, Aśvakandara at the rear gate;
Padmāntakṛt, the slayer of desire, who is whirled about by the fierce Vāgīśa. ||84||
In the north is Akṣobhya, the fierce destroyer of obstacles, and Amṛtakuṇḍalin;
Vighnāntakṛt [is placed there] for the sake of purifying the door-activities and the enemies of the gods. 85.
With furrowed brows, their hair, eyebrows, beards, and eyes blazing upward;
with distorted faces, lolling tongues, and baring fangs, they laughed fiercely. ||86||

These [deities] hold in their hands fierce mallets, staffs, lotuses, their own vajras, and so forth; their bodies are adorned with cruel serpents, and they are embraced by their respective consorts. ||87||

Having visualized the completed wheel in its own nature on all sides, one should draw in the Buddhas, who possess the luster of the seed-syllable in the heart, by means of hooks in the form of the wheel. (88)
Having seen the obstacles, having dispelled them with those that destroy one's own obstacles,
and having protected [the site], one should offer the *argha* water, over which the mantra has been recited, together with flowers dedicated to the moon and other deities.

Having placed that wheel within the circle, one should meditate upon it as being empowered by the eyes, body, and so forth, and as having been previously consecrated, ranging from the outflow [niṣyanda] up to the highest degree [adhimātra]. (90)
Akṣobhya is the crown of the Buddhas; the remaining [Buddhas] are consecrated by their own lords.
The gatekeepers are considered to be consecrated by the Lords of Body (Vairocana), Akṣobhya, and Speech (Amitābha), and the Lord of Mind (Amoghasiddhi). 91.
Thus, having poured [the offerings] with the radiance from one's own heart, the lotus of wisdom is established;
and form and the other [sensory objects], arising from the pores of the skin, are [offered] by means of the rays of Rūpavajrā and the others. (92)

Having worshipped himself and the lords of sages with rays emitted from the gabled pavilion that spread throughout the expanse of the sky, he becomes the very embodiment of the worship of those worthy of worship. (93)
Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra of worship of all Tathāgatas.
One should praise the wheel with all phenomena through the forms of the perfectly awakened ones' own bodies;
[one should praise] the five wisdoms with the mudrās, the five hundred families, and the triad. 94.
O Akṣobhyavajra, of great wisdom, Vajradhātu, Great Buddha, O Trimaṇḍala, supreme among the three vajras, Vajra of Sound, homage be to you! (95)
Vairocana, great purity, vajra peace, great delight;
O supreme among the supremely luminous by nature, homage be to you, Vajra of the [ten] directions! 96.
O King of Jewels, most profound, stainless as the vajra-space of the sky, pure by nature and untainted—homage be to you, Vajra Body! (97)
O Great King Vajrāmṛta, free from conceptual construction, holder of the space-vajra;
you who have attained the perfection of passion, O Bhāṣavajra, homage be to you! 98.
O perfectly awakened Amoghavajra, fulfiller of all hopes, born of the nature of purity, Vajrasattva, homage be to you! 99.
It resides within the moon, the sun, water, medicine, fragrance, wind, fire, and the wheel;
it is presided over by the Praṇava, accompanied by light, and consecrated with the three principles (tattvas). 100.

Having placed the *hūṃ* syllable on the tongue as a vajra and having meditated upon it as filled with the nectar of gnosis, one should satisfy the entire mandala situated within the moon at the heart by means of that [nectar]. ||101||

Having made the world consist of the nature of the Buddhas through Lords emanated from the light-rays of the heart—[Lords] who are free from their own false conceptualizations—one should cause it to enter within the seed-syllable of the heart. (102)

Having meditated upon one's own radiant mind as the Jñānasattva, situated within the seed-syllable at the center of the heart-mark—which takes the form of the moon and the bindu—one should cause it to shine forth. 103.
Having awakened the vajras of mind, speech, and body by means of a garland of rays, one should meditate upon her as she is seated in the heart, flowing with the nectar of one's own gnosis. (104)
Having illumined the entire interior body on all sides with that [light], one should fill the world for the sake of all beings with arrays of light radiating from every pore. (105)
Having meditated upon his own subtle insignia, or the wheel of the Sage situated at the tip of the nose of the Vidyā, which is self-cognizable and radiant through its union with true wisdom. (106)
Having seen the sign of stability, one should repeatedly perform the radiation [of light] by means of the signs of those rays, through various kinds of marks of the Buddhas. (107)
From the six vajras of body, speech, and mind, one should perform the recitation of the mantra that radiates rays of light from the five wisdoms, either simultaneously or sequentially. (108)
That wheel, which consists of the vajra of body, speech, and mind, is the adamantine covering; making its abode firm and radiating the gnosis-body (jñānakāya), one should perform the recitation. 109.
One should recite the mantra, expanded by the vital breaths and withdrawn through the measure of *māyā*;
one should perform the recitation (*jāpa*) in due order through the expansion and withdrawal of the body and other elements. (110)
Having thus uttered [the mantra] and pervaded the sky with those rays of light from his body and so forth,
emitting the flood of vidyās from his vital breath as before, he becomes worthy of the various offerings of the virtuous.

One should cause the flood of awakened consciousness— the stream of the command of the vital breath (*āyāma*)— which has been brought under control by the force of immersion in the bliss of the shimmering, perfectly hidden wisdom (*vidyā*), to enter into one's own self at the end. 112.
Through resolutions such as the flowing [of the drops], the drops are produced from the three secrets in a subtle manner;
likewise, the yogas are to be meditated upon through the distinctions of "mild" and so forth, just like the services (*sevā*) and the rest. //113//
Through the contemplation of the reality within one's own heart, having purified the limited movement of the mind,
one should worship and honor the maṇḍala with the songs sung by the assembly of Locanā and the other goddesses.
By duly causing the stream of the water of pure consciousness to fall upon the head—moist with the moon and the syllable Om—one should effect the gratification of body, speech, and mind. (115)

Having rested and performed the recitation (japa), the wise one, having completed the worship and other rites, should dismiss the Buddhas who have been withdrawn by means of the three principles (tritattva), being free from all attachment. 116.
Having thus observed the entire world as it is described by those who see reality, one should direct one's aspiration toward it out of compassion for its welfare. (117)
Arising from meditative absorption and maintaining pride toward his husband, he,
having entered the role of a spy, should thoroughly honor the spheres of the Perfectly Awakened One.

One should thus meditate upon the objects of the senses as being identical with the glorious Mañjuvajra, following their own nature, and as being established through the purity of each respective sense-object. (119)

Endowed with pure beings, he [visualizes] those who possess the nature of permanence and so forth, established in the dharmas of individual self-realization, appearing in the form of the glorious Vajradhara. (120)
Free from all improper intentions, one should accomplish every duty;
one should always worship the eternal wheel of reality and the immeasurable yogis. 121.

Having mentally grasped the Lord of one's own mandala within the moon at one's heart by means of one's own seed-syllables, one should transform all the Buddhas into nectar through the principles (tattvas) of one's own heart. 122.
Pure by virtue of the nature of all phenomena and consecrated with the three principles, one should worship while pleasing the true wheel of one's own tutelary deity with that [substance]. ||123||
This external person is to be inferred as consisting of mind alone, yet it is composed of the mental faculty;
however, this [person] is unsurpassed once the fuel of the aggregates has been consumed by the fire of primordial wisdom. ||124||

In this way, with all these very desires, one should worship others who are born from the essential nature of their respective deities; such is the commitment (samaya) intended by the Sugatas. //125//
Performing worship to all the Buddhas through those various actions of body and so forth, one should always act for the benefit of the world in a fitting manner, remaining concentrated. (126)
Whatever great action consisting of body and speech, which has the nature of mudrās and mantras, by performing each such action, one should worship all the Buddhas. ||127||
Since, with respect to a single object, various conceptual constructions appear in diverse forms, giving rise to liberation, suffering, and pleasure, and resulting in the entirety of karma; 128.
Therefore, virtuous and non-virtuous karma, consisting of body and so forth, arises from conceptual construction.
Since one is liberated from all unreal constructions through gnoses, how could there be such construction? (129)
Amoghavajrasaccakrī, for the sake of rousing the samaya, should meditate on the vajra-space of the heart-activity and consecrate [the disciple] through universal purity. ||130||
In the event of faults such as disrespect toward the guru, one should always perform a general feeding;
while remaining within one's own wheel, one should perform an external bath according to the procedure for consecration.
Even during the interval between the twilight prayers, having performed worship and recitation as before,
one should sleep while possessing wisdom and compassion, with the true wheel within the heart.
At the time of rising, the illustrious beginner, urged by the songs of the goddesses, should rise in the morning and recite [the mantra] as before. 133.

Endowed with mantras, moral conduct, and vows, and having consecrated his eyes, body, and so forth, one who has attained some degree of immersion in gnosis should recite [the mantra] during the twilights without sloth. (134)
One who has attained mastery over gnosis should constantly rely upon a yoga that is perfectly accomplished in all its aspects and performs the functions of emanation and withdrawal. (135)

Mastering right knowledge and meditating, he should perform deeds for the welfare of the world through the atoms of the elements, by means of the threefold wheels that are reflections of his own embodied form. (136)
Once the yogin has attained perfection, having repeatedly obtained the sign,
he should perform the ritual worship of the three principles according to the rules and then draw the mandala.
Having performed the recitation according to the rules while stationed upon the wheel— whether requested by himself or by another,
or even while striving for the sake of others— he should draw [the mandala] upon encountering the appropriate sign.
One should recite the mantra of the Discus-bearer (Cakrin) one hundred thousand times, or one hundred thousand times for one's own tutelary deity;
or, by the command of the Discus-bearer, one may correctly write [the mantras] of others ten thousand times each.

One should extract the mantras of the names by incorporating the three principles (tritattva) within the emission (utsarga), embedding them with the seed-syllable of the heart (hṛdbīja), and placing the nasalized vowel (anusvāra) at the beginning of each syllable. 140.
The secrets of body, speech, and mind are known as the great essence of action and phenomena; the pledge of the three secrets is the seal (mudrā), and the seed-syllable is called the heart. (141)
But it is said that the Vidyā is the agent of the action, because of the injunction for pacification and so forth;
and since the Mālā-mantras are also called Vidyās, the wise one should recite them in every way. (142)
Having performed the recitation as appropriate and having received permission from one's own lord and others,
one should draw [the mandala] after purifying one's own mind by resorting to the wheel of cessation.
Having dispelled the obstacles, sprinkled and purified the ground, and made supplications, one should request [permission];
then, having performed the threefold meditative absorption and consecrated the Buddhas and others, [one should proceed]. (144)
Having offered the bali and arghya, worshipped [the deity], and gratified [it] with oblations (homa), one should place [the deity] in the sky;
one should then cause the earth to be excavated so that it is free from obstacles—this same procedure applies even to the filling of the pit.
Having previously practiced the service [of the deity] and possessing the self-yoga of Mañjuvajra, one should consecrate the site of the maṇḍala together with companions, endowed with worship. (146)
Established in the yoga of the wheel of the enemy of obstacles, one should receive one's own consecration;
thus, one should indeed cut down the wicked through yoga or through one's own presiding deity.
With the mantra *oṃ bhūḥ khaṃ*, one should visualize the earth as being of the nature of space;
then, having transformed it into vajra-nature with *hūṃ laṃ hūṃ*, one should consecrate it.

Oṃ medinī vajrībhava vajrabandha hūṃ! As before, the practitioner of the yoga that destroys obstacles, who is impassioned from beginning to end, being the primordial yogi, should emit his own maṇḍala and become nectar. (149)

The self whose nature is the yoga of the foremost Wheel-King, who performs the rites of the wheel as excellent deeds—he is the yogin of the foremost King of Rites; such is the supreme triad of samādhis. 150.
Established in this yoga, the Master embodies the nature of all Buddhas;
with a vajra-nature pure by its very essence, he is situated in the center of the mandala ground. (151)

The Hero, holding the vajra and bell, having been requested for the manifestation of the three wheels, [is accompanied] by his assistants who hold the vajra and bell at their tips, and who have the forms of the essential natures of Śāśvata and the others. ||152||
Teach the supreme maṇḍala, which is quiescent and belongs to all Tathāgatas, the abode of all Tathāgatas, and the foremost selflessness of all phenomena. 153.
Complete with all auspicious marks and devoid of all inauspicious marks,
speak of the supreme mandala, the foremost body of Samantabhadra. (154)
Proclaim the supreme maṇḍala, born from the foremost of peaceful phenomena, which purifies the conduct of gnosis, and is the pinnacle of Samantabhadra’s speech. (155)
The great mind of all sentient beings is pure and naturally stainless;
it is the supreme mind of Samantabhadra, O Ghoṣa, charioteer of the maṇḍala! (156)
Then, seeing that the realm of sentient beings was shrouded in darkness, the King Mañjuśrī became enraged;
uttering "HŪṂ VAJROTTHĪṢṬHA," he cast upward the emanated wheel of his own eyes. (157)
With eyes like the moon and sun of Maṭkāra, illuminating all directions throughout the paths of time, the wise one should circumambulate the mandala ground while beholding the world. 158.
With a thunderbolt blazing from the soles of his feet, intent on brandishing the vajra, he dances the playful vajra-step, uttering the fierce *hūṃ* with his prominent fangs. ||159||
One should drive away the multitudes of the wicked, the circles of obstacles such as the gods and others.
Let all the hosts of obstacles residing in body, speech, and mind listen! (160)
I am the glorious Mañjurava, the one who employs the protection wheel;
with a vajra of blazing form, I shatter those born of the three bodies.
"If anyone should leap over me, he would be shattered here; it cannot be otherwise.
Having thus taken possession of the ground, one should drive stakes into it to ensure there are no obstacles. (162)

Oṃ gha gha, slay, slay all the wicked ones, phaṭ! Stake, stake all the sinful ones, phaṭ! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ, O Vajrakīla, Vajradhara commands you with the vajra of body, speech, and mind: stake him down, hūṃ phaṭ!
One should mentally stake the enemy obstacle-bearers from below with the spike at the top in the center.
One should destroy all the multitudes of obstacles situated throughout the ten directions. ||163||
Having surveyed the ground, which is free from obstacles and possesses a radiance filled with sharp flames,
one should perform the mental construction of the boundary, the enclosure wall, and the confinement of the directions, and then carry out the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
O Goddess, you are the witness of all the Buddhas, the Protectors, regarding the specificities of the methods of conduct and the stages and perfections. (165)
Just as the army of Māra was shattered by the Protector, the Lion of the Śākyas, so too, having conquered the army of Māra, I shall draw the maṇḍala. ||166||
Having smeared the ground with fragrant substances and the like, and having scattered various flowers,
the wise man should fashion a maṇḍala for the wielders of the discus (Viṣṇu) in the space beginning with the moon.
Having invoked [the deities] there, and having performed the wheel [of protection] along with the binding of the boundaries,
one should perform the worship, the praise, the tasting of nectar, and consecrate the vases. ||168||

One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) of the jars belonging to the deities of the mandala—whose necks are well-covered with cloth and which are provided with sprouts of mango and other trees—using their respective mantras. 169.

One should recite the *jaya* mantra while holding a collection of the five grains, medicinal herbs, jewels, fragrant water, and a wheel, with the head adorned by a vajra bound with garlands, under the command of the Lord of the Wheel.
Having offered the *argha* and performed worship, he should cast a white flower there,
along with a vessel containing lotuses and excellent perfumes, which has been scented with incense.
Having offered the bali offering daily at the three junctions of the day, one should likewise recite the mantra;
and they [the deities] are located in the outer corners of the wheel, with Jaya to the right of the Lord of the Wheel (Cakreśa).
Having poured water into the argha-vessel for them, by means of that [water], there shall be a water-consecration for oneself and for all the disciples. ||173||
Having performed the worship of the wheel again and raising incense with his hand, the wise one, kneeling on the ground, should pray to the Lord of the Wheel and to the Buddhas. (174)
O Blessed One, Mañjuśrīvajra, King of Vidyās, homage be to you!
O Protector, I desire to write down the mandala whose nature is compassion. (175)
Out of compassion for my disciples and for your own honor, O Blessed One, you ought to show favor to me, your devotee. (176)
May the Buddhas, who bestow the purpose of the wheel of activity for the world, and the Bodhisattvas established in the fruit, as well as all other mantra-deities, attend to me. (177)
The deities, the world-protectors, and the spirits who have been instructed in perfect awakening—whatever beings there may be who delight in the teaching and possess the vajra-eye. (178)
I, [name], the Great Vajrin, shall draw the arising maṇḍala of Mañjuśrī for the purification of the world, according to my capacity and with due offerings. (179)
Out of compassion, may he together with his disciples be pleased with me; all of you, being assembled in this maṇḍala, should deign to grant your presence.

Having thus invited them three times and performed the worship and other rites for the Lord, and having secured [the site] and gone outside with his disciples who hold the ends of his garment, [he should proceed]. (181)
[He should appoint] wise men who possess great energy, who are grateful, free from egoism, of noble birth, virtuous, faithful, and endowed with beauty, complexion, and youth. (182)

One should provide hospitality even to those who are destitute, those who are accused, those who follow the Sugata in the practice of mantras, as well as those who are deformed, devoid of virtues, or lowly. (183)
The ritual procedure for the mandala is authorized for all four assemblies—those who are engaged in their respective trainings and whose minds delight in the Mahāyāna. (184)
Some enter this mandala seeking the accomplishment of mantras;
others do so desiring merit, and still others seek the welfare of the next world. (185)
A wise person, having set their intention upon the next world and having developed great faith, should enter the maṇḍala; they should not seek worldly results.
For one who desires this world, the fruit of the next world is not so great; but for a man seeking the next world, the fruit of this world is indeed abundant. (187)
Having spoken thus to those disciples who have been inwardly established by his mind,
and who— as before— have been purified by the vajra-lotus, he should request them at the door of the house.
You are my teacher, O Great Joyful One; [O Ācārya, attend to me!
O Great Protector, I desire the firm method of Great Awakening.
Grant me the commitment; grant me the reality and the bodhicitta.
Grant me the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha—the Three Refuges. ||190||
"O Lord, lead me into the supreme city of great liberation.
Having spoken this three times and having recognized that the disciples were devoted to him, [he led them in]. (191)

Having first made one disciple, he should speak these words: "Come, child! I shall correctly teach you the method of the practice of mantra within the Mahāyāna; for you are a worthy vessel for the Great Way. (192)
The Buddhas, arisen throughout the three times, possess the vajras of body, speech, and mind;
they have attained incomparable gnosis through the cultivation of vajra mantras. (193)
By means of this incomparable application of mantra, the great and most terrible army of Māra was shattered by the excellent ones, such as the Lion of the Śākyas.
Having conformed to worldly convention and set the wheel of Dharma in motion, they have attained nirvāṇa;
therefore, my child, apply your mind to this [path] for the sake of attaining omniscience. (195)

Having caused [the disciple] to recite the confession and so forth three times, the Guru should then generate the bodhicitta that has not yet been generated, or cause that which has already been generated to be remembered once more. (196)
Having performed all the rites of protection, one should meditate upon the heart, throat, and head;
one should place the vajra, the lotus, and likewise the wheel, along with the syllables HŪṂ, ĀḤ, and OṂ, within them. 197.
Reciting "HŪṂ OM ĀḤ" while holding a fistful of scented water and vajras, and touching the heart, head, and throat, one should offer flowers and so forth in succession. (198)

The ascetic should reverently bestow upon the disciples flowers on the head, incense before them, a lamp, and perfume again upon the heart—each having been consecrated with the recitation of the Sarvakṛt mantra. (199)

One should provide a tooth-stick made from the wood of the *aśvattha* or *udumbara* trees, twelve finger-breadths in length, with its tip intact by flowers, free from insects, unblemished, and not crooked. (200)

Having first smeared the ground to the extent of a *gocarma* with those [substances] placed facing east and north, one should cast [the materials] into it; this bestows success such as pacification and the like.
Having sipped water and given three mouthfuls of water for rinsing, and having seated him outside,
one should well-protect the arms with threads for the sake of a bed and pillow made of *kuśa* grass. (202)
The mantra for drinking the three nectars: Oṃ hrīḥ, O Pure Dharma, purify all the sins of this person; remove all conceptual constructions, hūṃ!
When does the appearance of the All-Knowing One arise in the world, or does it not? [It is as rare] as that of the udumbara tree.
Or perhaps a flower might appear at some time or another. ||203||
Even rarer than that is the arising of the way of mantra practice, by which those who have not yet passed into nirvana are indeed able to accomplish incomparable benefit for sentient beings. (204)
Whatever evil was committed in the past over many millions of eons, all of that indeed goes to destruction upon seeing such a maṇḍala. (205)
How much more so for one who abides in the system of mantra practice and possesses infinite glory;
for by reciting the mantra of the Protectors, one indeed attains the unsurpassed state. (206)
The miserable states of existence, which are the source of all suffering, have been cut off for those whose minds are utterly pure regarding this most excellent conduct. (207)
Today, O great-souled ones, you have obtained incomparable gains, in that you have been [established] here in this teaching by all the Victors together with their sons. (208)
All of you, as you were being born, were taken into the care of great beings;
therefore, tomorrow you shall indeed be born into the Mahāyāna. (209)
This is the glorious, supreme path, the great success of the Mahāyāna; by means of it, you shall go forth and become Tathāgatas.
Having performed the teaching of the purpose and the protection ritual, one should have them sleep on a bed of *kuśa* grass, saying:
"Whatever you see in a dream, you shall tell me in the morning. (211)
Having performed the protection, empowerment, and so forth, one should recite that which is effective for all rites.
Kuṇḍalī, belonging to the five families and the three wheels, is effective for all rites. (212)

Having inquired about auspicious and inauspicious dreams and having destroyed inauspiciousness by means of the *kuṇḍalī*, he should then cause those worthy disciples whom he has protected to undertake the vow (*saṃvara*). ||213||
O Lord, having bestowed the consecration of the irreversible wheel, please tell me the reality of the wheel and its deity, as well as the preparatory rites for the preceptor.
The commitment of all Buddhas, the supreme secret vow:
"May I always be an Ācārya for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings. (215)
Having caused the disciples who seek the state of a teacher to grasp the vow,
and having performed yoga, he should worship the true wheel and place it in the sky with his mind.
The thread, which appears in the form of eternity and so forth, arises from the seed-syllables of those colors;
it is endowed with the five gnoses and is divided into twenty-five parts. (217)

He whose eyes are the sun and moon arising from the syllable YAṂ, whose body is the very form of Mañjuvajra, draws [the object] with a blazing gaze like a hook and causes it to enter within his own color. (218)
Together with Sarvakṛtā, bestow the wisdom-thread of the hearts of Vairocana and the others, as well as the thread of Śāśvata, for the purpose of marking out one's own mandala. (219)
While seeking the goal as far as Akṣobhya, who is indeed encapsulated by the three principles, one should recollect that "all phenomena are mutually interpenetrating," and so forth. ||220||
Twice as long as the wheel, it should be one-twentieth the width of the door;
having moistened it with the five nectars and fragrant substances, it is then protected.
The yogi should cause that which is contained within the three syllables to revolve by means of the thread-holder;
having sent it forth with the sounds *tri-jaḥ*, he himself should again utter *jjaḥ jjaḥ jjaḥ*. (222)
Holding his left fist at the navel, the illustrious one stands facing the western direction;
he should cast the sky-line and likewise project the lower line.
Oṃ vajrasamayasūtraṃ mātikrama hūṃ! For the sake of sentient beings, O Tathāgatas who pervade space, urge yourselves with the sound of the thread [of the ritual] to come here. ||224||

Having first laid out the threads for the four directions—east, west, north, and south—and for the exterior, [marking] the quarters of the Yakṣas, Pretas, Indras, and Nāgas, as well as those resting on fire and wind. 225.
Having laid out the diagonal lines,
one situated in the southeast and southwest [corners] should likewise mark the eight circles in the directions of east, west, north, and south.
Having doubled that thread and fixed it within the centers of the wheels, one should then [draw] two vajra-threads outside in the shape of a wheel. (227)
In the northeast, the wise one, maintaining equality in all directions, should mark out the Cakravāḍa mountain by means of a thread, proceeding clockwise according to the proper sequence. (228)
If the signs are absent, there will be no accomplishment; if the thread is broken, the preceptor perishes.
From deficiency or excess [in measurement], diseases arise; from confusion regarding the directions, the disciple falls into delusion. ||229||
It is square, with four gates, adorned with four archways, provided with four [boundary] lines, and decorated with silk bands and garlands of flowers. ||230||
In all the corner sections and at the junctions of the doorways and projections,
one should mark out the outer maṇḍala, inlaid with vajra-jewels.
Inside of that is a wheel resembling eight circles, circular in shape all around, with a radius equal to half that of the outer wheel. ||232||

One should divide the auspicious [mandala], which is fashioned with wheel-pillars and the like and surrounded by a garland of vajras, starting from the door by means of the syllable *Hrīḥ* and the wrathful gaze. (233)
The door is considered to be one-eighth of the wheel's diameter and is devoid of a vedikā;
the niryūhas and the deity-paṭṭikās are equal in measure to the door.
The half-door, the altar on all sides, the cheek, and likewise the wing;
the necklace, the half-necklace, the moon, the sun, the fillet, the garland-band, and the molding. 235.
The ground for the powder-line is half of that; the root-sūtra is outside the ground.
The ground for the sūtras of the first pillar of the wheel and so forth is equal to the ground for the powder-line.
The archway (toraṇa) should be three times the width of the door and be provided with flags and bells;
the flags, stirred by the wind from the excellent bells, [should hang] from the outer corners.
For others, the arrangement is according to the wheel and as is aesthetically pleasing;
because he is the wisdom-body of the Perfectly Awakened One, he is known as the eloquent one in the Vajra family. ||238||

Regarding the complete purification of the self as the Dharmakāya, the maṇḍala of his mind, having taken account of the dispositions of sentient beings, established the rules concerning pride and so forth. ||239||
Since accomplishment arises from wisdom and means, why is there a restriction regarding caste and so forth?
[This applies] starting from one cubit up to a thousand cubits. (240)
Having thus outlined that wheel, one should consecrate and empower the powders with a blazing gaze and the excellent radiance of the knowledge-mantra of the preceding rite.
Oṃ vajracittatra samaya hūṃ!
This is the pure dharmadhātu, which liberates the realm of sentient beings;
it is King Mañjurava himself, the abode of all Tathāgatas. (242)
Completely free from all defects and situated within the circle, the Guru, facing the northeastern direction, [should act] with his left fist. (243)
One should draw lines that are white, yellow, red, green, and black respectively, equal in width, clockwise, unbroken, and straight. 244.
One should lay down a level line divided into twenty parts for the door;
if it falls thick, there will be disease, and with one that is thin, there is the loss of wealth. (245)
If it is crooked, there is enmity; if severed, death for both teacher and disciple;
and if it falls in a non-circumambulatory direction, there will be the immobilization of the menstrual flow.
One needle is made of white vajra, another has a golden base;
one needle is made of ruby, and likewise another of emerald. (247)
This sequence of colors for it should be known as being within the black [area]:
to the east is great white, and to the south it is joined with yellow.
The western part is red, joined with madder-red in the north;
in the center, however, the ground portion is radiant with the luster of sapphire.
One who is well-composed should always draw [the mandala] consisting of wisdom and means;
the lines should be drawn so that there is an interval of one barley-corn between them. 450.
Crushing all the wicked with the vajra of the nectar of the earring, this King of Mantras is called Mahāmudrāsya-daṃṣṭra, the enemy of the wicked. 451.
Homage to all the Vajras of Body, Speech, and Mind!
Homage to Vajrakrodha, the Great Fanged One, Terrifying with His Exalted Fangs, who holds a sword, a club, a spear, and a noose in his hands!
Oṃ Amṛtakuṇḍali! Kha kha khāhi khāhi! Tiṣṭha tiṣṭha! Bandha bandha! Hana hana! Daha daha! Garja garja! Visphoṭaya visphoṭaya all obstructors and Vināyakas!
HŪṂ PHAṬ! To the one who brings an end to the life of Mahāgaṇapati!
Having thus drawn the maṇḍala, with a seat formed by the moon and sun, one should draw a dark blue sword in the center, radiant with the purity of the primordial nature. 252.
To the east is the wheel of truth with eight spokes, brilliantly radiant like a mirror and other such objects;
on the right is the jewel, greenish in luster, possessing nine facets, and perfectly even and elevated.
In the west is an eight-petalled lotus, red, representing discerning awareness (pratyavekṣā-jñāna) and so forth;
in the north is a sword, adorned with the [four] activities (kṛtya) and so forth. ||254||
By means of skillful methods, one should place the Eye in the southeast; by petitioning, the Vajra in the southwest;
and by force, the lotus with its stalk and its blossoming face in the northwest. (255)
In the northeast, from wisdom, there is a yellow lotus, beautiful like a dark blue cloud;
[it is located] in the four corners beginning with the southeast, and on both sides of the eastern gate. (256)
Likewise, a mirror, a lute, perfume, a conch, an elixir, clothing, and the source of dharma (dharmodaya), all purified by generosity, ethical discipline, and the other perfections. ||257||
Having thoroughly understood and clearly visualized the hammer of faith and the rest, as well as the staff, lotus, and fourthly the vajra at the gates, one should visualize one's own wheel.
As before, through the union with the limbs of wisdom, having caused the Buddhas to enter within oneself,
one pervades space with the true mind, establishing their dwellings at the sides of the wheel.
Having dispelled those obstacles that have arrived with them and having protected [the site],
one should draw [the deity] in by means of Yamāri and others, cause [him] to enter, bind [him], and bring [him] under control.
Having presided over the eyes, body, and so forth, and having performed the offering of water, consecration, and worship;
then, having praised, gladdened, recited the mantra, and meditated, one should satisfy [the deity]. ||261||
As before, having placed the nectar of gnosis into the vessel of the lotus,
and having worshipped the guardians of the directions established in their respective yogas, one should enter the mandala.
Having become Trailokyavijaya, adorned with ornaments and garments as obtained,
and having performed a circumambulation and bowed to the wheel, one should complete [the rite] with an oblation.

Having abandoned the fruit of the fourfold [measure], that which measures one cubit or half a cubit below it is to be known as the "all-purpose" [mandala], like a wheel, for the sake of causing the lotus of pride to blossom. (264)
One should draw a sword measuring eight or nine finger-breadths in both length and height,
situated within a wheel, a jewel, and a lotus, in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

The yogin, standing facing the east, having recited the mantra while surrounded by an outer circle of vajras, should protect all that has been done; on his left side he should place the water for offering (argha) and other items as appropriate. (266)

Having arranged the ritual implements and sprinkled them with water, one who possesses the yoga of the nature of Mañjuvajra [should prepare] a fire ignited by fuel from milk trees, purified by the three syllables.
Having kindled [the fire] with fanning blows, one should offer *kuśa* grasses while circumambulating to the right;
the seed-syllable *raṃ*, which resides in the heart of the first [deity],
is situated within a triangle and a lotus.
The arising from the seed. ||268||

Having meditated upon the yellow [deity] with three faces, stout, embracing the body of Prajñā, and holding a water-pot, the gesture of fearlessness, a staff, and a rosary in his hands—[one should worship] Anala here. (269)
Having invoked the fire of true gnosis as before with the *tritattva-ṭakki* mantra,
one should perform its sprinkling and other rites, and then seat it upon its throne.
Below the handle of the ladle (*hastadaṇḍa*) it is square, and above that it is adorned with *vajra* jewels;
the bowl is four finger-breadths wide, with a hollow two finger-breadths deep below the *vajra*. (271)
At a distance of four finger-breadths from the edge of the vajra, there is the shape of a lotus petal;
it is hollowed out by one finger-breadth for the inner vajra, and its stem is two finger-breadths long. ||272||
Having meditated upon one's own deity as a blazing seed-syllable within the mouths of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles,
one should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) to it, having placed the letter *ra* (repha) in its mouth.
The virtuous one should offer fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sesame seeds,
pieces of dūrvā grass, curd-rice, and kuśa grass into the kindled fire, following the prescribed order.

Having first performed the external worship and other preliminaries, one should meditate upon the syllable *maṃ*, the Lord of Existence, within the moon of the heart; this is the true wheel of the excellent fire of the knowledge of suchness, which one should offer as an oblation. (275)
Om, svāhā to Agni;
[this is] of clarified butter.
Oṃ, to the vajra that burns all sins, burn all sin, svāhā!
[For sesame seeds.]
Oṃ vajrāyuṣe svāhā | [This is] for the dūrvā grass.
Oṃ vajrapuṣṭaye svāhā | [This is the mantra] for unbroken rice grains.
Oṃ, for all prosperity, svāhā! [This is] for the curd-rice.
Oṃ apratihatavajrāya svāhā | [This is for] the kuśa grasses.
For nourishment, pacification, subjugation, attraction, hatred, expulsion, and malevolent rites, the incitement at the end of the mantra is: Oṃ svāhā hoḥ jaḥ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ. (276)
"By means of the heart-sattva and the self-lord, all the deities are gratified.
Thus meditating, one should satisfy them with the moon and other substances as before. (277)

Having likewise offered the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the tongue [of fire] upon the moon-wheel of the heart, and having sprinkled [the deity], given water for sipping (ācamana), the respectful offering (argha), worshipped, and praised, one should dismiss [the deity]. ||278||
Having offered the remaining oblation into the fire by means of his own yoga,
and having likewise dismissed him according to the previous procedure, he should worship the wheel and then lie down to rest.
Having first entered by means of the ritual for the initiation of disciples, the adept himself,
having performed [the rites] up to the consecration (seka), obtains permission from the lords of the family (kulādhipa).
The reality arising from great passion and the maṇḍala are like a reflection;
for the sake of admitting the disciple into the city, one should proclaim that reality and the truth. (281)
Because he is the sign of the arising of space, the supreme one is without beginning or end;
may the Being consisting of the great vajra, Mañjuvajra, be accomplished for me today. (282)
O supreme among all, great accomplishment, presiding deity of great sovereignty!
O King who holds all vajras, may you grant me the perfection of the supreme syllable. (283)
You are faultless and eternal, O you who inspire passion for all passions;
in truth, O Blessed One, you are the Great Passion and the Great Joy. (284)
The Tathāgata, who is the ultimate purity of all that is foremost and is liberated from the beginning, is Samantabhadra, the self of all; he is the Bodhisattva renowned to me. (285)
By means of the supreme seal of sovereignty, the highest of all great accomplishments, O Vajra of the Siddhas, through your great excellence, may the pride of the Vajra descend upon me. (286)
Pervading the minds of all beings, abiding in the hearts of all beings, and indeed the father of all beings, Kāma is the foremost of those who possess the supreme commitment (samaya). 287.
By that truth through which the maṇḍala, consisting of wisdom and skillful means, is true gnosis—by that truth, O Protector, fulfill my desires! (288)
All phenomena are like reflections; they are transparent, pure, and unclouded.
They are ungraspable and inexpressible, yet they arise from causes and karma. ||289||
"Since suchness has emerged from reality, by this truth, may all the disciples, free from stain, clearly behold the reflection within the mandala. (290)

Having sprinkled the disciple— who possesses the general vows and whose body and so forth are luminous as before— into the space between the birth-giving [mother] and the womb, as well as all the ritual vessels, one who performs all rites [should proceed]. (291)
O beloved, he should then ask that red-clad one with the face [of Kālarātri], "Who are you?
To which the disciple should reply, O beloved, "I am Subhaga. (292)
Having honored the door-keeper at the entrance and likewise having given him a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
one should generate the mind of yoga and place the vajra at the heart with the heart-mantra.
The mantra: Oṃ, I generate the mind of all yoga; O Surata, you are the pledge! Hoḥ! Be accomplished, O Vajra, as you please!
Today you shall be empowered by all the Tathāgatas.
You must not speak of this supreme secret of all the Tathāgatas to one who has not entered the maṇḍala, nor should it be given to one who lacks faith—thus it should be said.

Having summoned and caused [the guests] to enter by means of their own mantras beginning with *yamāryā*, one should likewise speak thus during the reception of the true vows (*saṃvara*) using the five syllables. (294)
Today you have entered the family of all the Tathāgatas.
Therefore, I shall generate in you the vajra-wisdom by means of which you shall attain even the accomplishments of all the Tathāgatas, let alone other accomplishments.
You must not speak of this before anyone who has not seen the maṇḍala.
Having placed a vajra in his heart with the thought, "May your commitment not be violated (or rendered futile)," [the teacher says]:
"Oṃ! Vajrasattva himself is today established within your heart. (295)
If he should speak this method, one should instantly pierce through and cause him to drink the five nectars located within the lotus, radiant with the three syllables. (296)
This water of yours, belonging to the hell realms, would burn you for transgressing the pledge;
through the preservation of the pledge, there is accomplishment—drink this vajra-amṛta water! (297)
Oṃ vajrodaka ṭhaḥ.
One should speak these words to one who is firm in their vow:
"From this day forward, I am Vajrapāṇi to you; whatever I tell you to do, that must be performed by you.
You must not disregard me, lest, by failing to avoid misfortune, you should bring about your own death and fall into hell."
Then he should say to the disciples:
"May all the Tathāgatas empower [you], and may Vajrasattva enter into me! And having had them recite this, [he places it] upon their hearts.
One should meditate on a yellow *hūṃ* marked with a vajra in the Āndhra (northeast) corner;
there should be a white *vaṃ* marked with a jar in the circular [corner] of Varuṇa (west). (298)
The Vāyavya [mantra] is marked with a blue banner, resembling a bow, and consists of the syllable *yaṃ*; it is mobile and belongs to Bhava.
For the body and speech, there are *haḥ* and *āḥ* respectively; beneath the feet is *jhraiḥ*, which is brilliantly blazing. (299)
In the northwest, [visualize] *raṃ* as Bhava; having kindled it with a triangle, one should cause it to enter the disciple.
Recite: "Cause to enter! Cause to tremble! *ra-ra-ra-ra*, move! *2 hūṃ haḥ āḥ jhaiḥ*! (300)
Having meditated on a red syllable ĀḤ on the tongue, one should speak again to the possessed person:
"O Rāgavajra, having taken hold of him, tell me, O Vajra, what is auspicious and what is inauspicious. (301)
Stabilizing that possession, one should say, "O Vajra, remain!
One should cast the garland into the wheel and say, "Accept it, O Vajra! Hoḥ! ||302||
One should bind it upon the head [with the mantra]: "O Being of Great Power, accept this being!
[Whether] near the signs or not, for both those who have surrendered and those who have not. (303)
Whether out of faith or because of their spiritual fitness, one should bestow that yoga;
having meditated on the flaming *praṇava* in the eyes.
Oṃ! Today Vajrasattva himself is intent upon opening your eyes;
he opens that which is the unsurpassed vajra-eye, which perceives all. (305)
One should display the wheel. ||304||
Beginning with the Lord of the Mandala and continuing as far as Amṛtakuṇḍalin,
one should sprinkle water upon their heads while uttering the words of the vajra-consecration.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] with the crown as before, and having offered the presiding deity,
one should grasp that vajra at the heart and consecrate him with the vajra.
Today you have been consecrated by the Buddhas through the vajra-consecration.
Take this, which is the state of all Buddhahood—the vajra—for the sake of perfect accomplishment. (308)
Embracing with the vajra and bell, from one's own lord:
"Oṃ, I consecrate you as the Vajra Lord; abide as you, the Vajra Samaya!
Oṃ, Vajrasattva, I consecrate you through the vajra-name consecration."
O such-and-such Vajra!
[I address you] by name upon the crown of your head:
whatever shines as one's own entire possession, that which is primary is Mañjurāṭ himself.
For phenomena are pure by nature; indeed, that is the accumulation of the Buddha’s wisdom. //309//
In one's own state as a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), the name begins with "Śrī" and ends with "Vajra"; all [deities] are thus assigned to the position of supreme lordship over everything. (310)
The purity of the water element is Akṣobhya; the crown is of the nature of equanimity.
The vajra is of the nature of authentic discerning awareness; it is the sovereign who performs purposeful action and bestows benefit. (311)
In this context, knowledge (*jñāna*) is the *vidyā*, the *vajra* is the element (*dhātu*), and the one who has been mastered is the lineage (*gotra*).
These—vow, prophecy, and consolation—are also present in the name during the *vidyā*-consecration. (312)
This is that state of omniscient buddhahood, which resides in the hand of Vajrasattva;
you too, O Vajrapāṇi of firm vows, must always uphold it. (313)
Oṃ! O Vajrasamaya of the accomplishment of all Tathāgatas, abide! I hold you fast! Hīḥ hi hi hi hi hūṃ!
Having bestowed the Vajra-vow upon all, one should cause them to grasp the Vajra in its true essence:
"The Being without beginning or end is Vajrasattva, the Great Joy. (314)
Samantabhadra, the universal self, the Lord of Vajragarva, the Sovereign—having grasped the bell in its true essence, one should sound it with the sound of the Dharma. ||315||
This is known as the resonance of the wisdom of all Buddhas;
it should always be maintained by you as well, for awakening is considered supreme by the Victors.
One should sound it according to that dharma. ||316||
For existence is pure by its very nature, yet it is rendered non-existent by [conceptual] natures;
when noble beings are pure by their very nature, they bring about supreme existence. (317)

Having empowered the Mahāmudrā through the heart-mantras proclaimed for service and so forth, one should recite the mantra without deficiency by means of the commitments (samayas) such as Kāmarūpa and the others. ||318||

Through those [deities] whose nature is self-cognizable, who abide in all directions and the three times, one should worship oneself and others by means of the yoga with one's own presiding deity. ||319||

By those difficult observances and restraints, when practiced, the accomplishments are not attained—namely, invisibility, the superknowledges, and the powers arising from speech, mind, and body, such as traveling through the sky. (320)
Therefore, the Buddhas and the true beings who practice the supreme conduct of mantra have attained the most excellent syllable of Dharma through the enjoyment of all desires. (321)

While enjoying the five strands of sensual pleasure, which consist of the nature of happiness, suffering, and both, one who seeks knowledge should indeed accomplish everything through union with those possessed of passion. (322)

Through the perfect accomplishment of body, speech, and mind, even those other [attainments] known as inferior are achieved by means of mantra recitation and the meditations on body, speech, and mind. ||323||
As it has been said:

"Having grasped the vajra according to its true nature and sounding the bell according to the Dharma, and having empowered the Mahāmudrā through the Samaya, one should recite the mantra from the heart. (324)
To this it was replied:
"Having received the vows and likewise having offered the ritual fee (dakṣiṇā), one should request initiation after bowing with this verse: [325]
Just as the great festival was bestowed upon the Buddhas by Bodhivajra, so too, for the sake of my protection, O Khavajra, grant it to me today! (326)

One should visualize the eight yogins situated upon the pedestals at the entrance doors of the lotus with eight petals, together with the wheels of Buddhas born from one's own heart, which pervade all directions, the three times, and space. (327)
Accompanied by music, incense, and other offerings as before, one should consecrate the recipient of the Vidyā-consecration with the Great Vajra Consecration, according to the verse: ||328||
I bestow the great vajra consecration, which is honored by the three realms and arises from the abode of the three secrets of all the Buddhas. (329)
Having bestowed the consecration of non-retrogression, one should reveal the reality of the wheel;
it is square because of its lack of inequality, due to the equality of the awakened and the unawakened. (330)
Because body, sensation, mind, and phenomena are not joined with multiplicity or unity, the mindfulness directed toward them and the faith therein are considered the gateway to awakening. (331)

Then, for the sake of abandoning and preventing the arising of misconceptions regarding what has occurred and what will occur, and furthermore, for the sake of the arising and stability of the reality that has arisen from what was non-existent; ||332||
The western gate consists of the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*): vigor, aspiration, exertion, and stability; however, mindfulness is the faculty therein. (333)

The incomparable faculties and powers of faith, vigor, mindfulness, meditative concentration, and wisdom, as well as supreme samādhi—thus, through the faculties of mindfulness, there are four gates. (334)
By means of the four dhyānas beginning with the first, it becomes like a structure with four archways (toraṇa);
the śūraṅgama, khagagañja, and other samādhis are known as the railings (vedikā). (335)
On the altar, there is a multitude of women holding garlands and other items, busily engaged in performing worship;
because of those variegated ornaments, all desires are fulfilled.
It resounds with the voice of the ninefold True Dharma shaken forth by the Vinaya, and it is made to ring by the bells upon the world’s foremost banners stirred by the wind. (337)
With the factors of enlightenment consisting of wisdom and mirrors, shining in all directions, it is radiant with necklaces, half-necklaces, the moon, the sun, mirrors, garlands, and chowries. (338)
By means of the six pillars beginning with the wheel-jewel, which are purified by the eight liberations, there is within that [mandala] a circle resembling eight mandalas. (339)
Because it sets in motion the Vajrayāna for all directions and the three times, it is encircled by vajra-lines, perfectly circular on all sides. ||340||

The five colors are the five perfectly awakened ones, because they delight sentient beings through the [five] gnoses; and because, through the complete purification of the sense faculties, their objects, and so forth, there is a discernment of all characteristics. (341)
The nectar of the wisdom-knowledge has been drunk by the Vajra-holders; that is the vase.
The full pitcher is the outflow of the completion of the accumulations, moistened by compassion. (342)

And that which is known as the flowers, incense, great lamps, and perfumes in the mandala is an accumulation of the factors of enlightenment, the fragrance of the mind, the torch of Dharma, and glory. (343)
The food offering consists of the Dharma; modesty and shame are the garments;
and well-sung songs, dances, and instrumental music increase great bliss. (344)
Because it is the city of liberation, it is the city; because it is a compendium of the essential, it is the mandala.
Having demonstrated the reality of the wheel, one should point out the reality of the deity. (345)
Through the purity of faith, vigor, mindfulness, meditative concentration, and [the five] purities, it has the form of the six waters;
through the purity of wisdom, the mind that perceives yoga regarding the body and so forth is perfectly stainless. (346)
Through the purification external to the six perfections beginning with generosity, one maintains the meditative cultivation of Rūpavajrā and the others;
because of the absence of signs such as earth, water, and so forth, it has the intrinsic nature of Locanā and the other goddesses. (347)
Through the purity of knowledge regarding objects, sentient beings, self, conceptualization, and activity, there arises a mirror-like cognition that is the very nature of all Buddhas. (348)
Through the yoga of the non-arising of cognition, [one perceives] the luminous form of the Lord of the Mandala;
through the complete purification of delusions regarding form and so forth, [one perceives] the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements. //349//
Through the transformation of stinginess and other [defilements], it is supremely firm in the highest elements;
through the transformation of its own opposites, it is complete and stainless, possessing power and the rest. (350)
But because it is non-conceptual, it possesses profundity; and because it brings about the welfare of both self and others, it possesses magnificence.
Through this profundity and magnificence, the mind is considered to consist of wisdom and skillful means. (351)
Because it is a reality to be personally realized within oneself, it does not abide as either differentiated or non-differentiated;
when explained in this way, the fruits such as the perfections (pāramitās) and so forth appear. //352//

Then, having performed the yoga with the foremost of the pledges (samayāgryā) conjoined with the qualities of the ocean of forms, the preceptor, having entered therein, should effect the immersion of gnosis (jñānāveśa). ||353||
Having struck the lotus with the vajra and drawn the Buddhas within himself,
and having stabilized those residing upon the lotus, he receives permission from the Lord of the Family.
Uttering his own name, the Vajra-being should emanate [the deities] through the yoga of the wheel;
having summoned the Buddhas by means of the sounds of the vajra and lotus, he should bring them to the sides of the wheel. (355)
Having dispelled the obstacles, protected [the site], offered the *argha* water, and performed full worship, one should praise [the deities] and,
having performed the rite of the gateway with the gatekeepers, accomplish [the practice] here.

In this rite imagined through the empowerment, sprinkling, worship, and so forth of the eyes, body, and other parts, one should inform [the deities]: "Act for the sake of all sentient beings and for the attainment of all siddhis! (357)
Having properly drawn the wheel, this is the procedure for the initial consecration;
however, for images, books, and so forth, it extends up to the *pauruṣa* rite following the sprinkling.
The rites for the water-pot, the offering of arghya, the canopy, and so forth, as well as the protective fire-oblation (rakṣāhoma) and other such acts that have been prescribed,
should be performed with the excellent mantras of three or five syllables, or with the mantras previously extracted.
Having performed the external bath himself like a universal monarch (cakravartin),
he realizes that this indeed is the supreme reality, which consists of wisdom and skillful means.

The water-consecration is the *niṣyanda* (outflow); the consecration called "Lord of the Vajra" is the *pāka* (ripening). The *pauruṣa* (human effort) consecration is performed by the Perfect Buddhas, while the *vaimalya* (stainless) consecration arises from the secret yoga. ||361||

Then, having empowered that woman—who was endowed with beauty and other qualities, who was well-practiced in the yoga of the wheel, and who abided by the commitments and vows—I placed her upon the wheel. ||362||

Having caused the host of lords of sages to enter within the vajra and having experienced true bliss, one should press with the Anāmikā and Jyeṣṭhā fingers and cause [the essence] to fall into the mouth of the disciple.
The disciple of firm intellect should drink everything with the nature of Vairocana;
he becomes the universe itself, like the universe—exclaiming, "Oh, what bliss! (364).
Through contact with wisdom, the illustrious one shall clearly perceive reality;
this delightful dhāraṇī of yours is to be cultivated, as ordained by the Buddhas. (365)
Through the application of the sequence of the wheel, taste the sublime bliss, while observing the mind within the jewel from the vajra-paryaṅka posture. (366)

Having explained the mandala, the reality of the deity, and the purification of the preceptor, and having consecrated [the disciple] with the secret and wisdom [empowerments], one should point out the reality.

As it is said: "Neither through the conduct of awakening and other such virtuous methods, nor by any other means, are all the Buddhas and so forth attained as they are through the method beginning with initiation. (368)
One should guard the commitment (*samaya*) toward one’s master and always maintain the vow (*saṃvara*). The five meats and nectar (*amṛta*) are to be consumed; [the master] is to be protected.
Therefore, there is also another convention. ||369||

The destruction of those who destroy jewels, the enjoyment of all women and others' property, and false speech—this indeed must be observed according to the rules, as it is remembered in the Yoga-tantra. (370)
Then, having become a Tathāgata, one should grant the prophecy with this song:
the left hands hold the heart, the fist, and the robe, while the right hands bestow the boon. (371)
Oṃ! Here I am, the Tathāgata Vajrasattva, prophesying for you so that, having been extracted from the miserable states of existence, you may achieve the ultimate perfection of being. (372)
He is the Tathāgata named Vajra for the sake of accomplishment; *bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ*.
By this [mantra], the practitioner who is the lord of the entire world is prophesied;
indeed, even the Sugatas would prophesy him for unsurpassed enlightenment. (373)
For in whatever way sentient beings proceed according to their own nature, in that very way one who is pure through passion and the rest should act for the sake of sentient beings. (374)
Practicing the yoga of the three samādhis four times every day at the junctions of the day,
achieve the perfection that consists of both the common and the extraordinary meditations.
In a thousandfold world-system one has the power of invisibility; in two thousandfold systems, one possesses the superknowledges (*abhijñā*);
in three thousandfold systems, one is a Vidyādhara; and as the Lord of the entire world, one is a Vajrī. ||376||
Whatever rite there may be—be it pacification, nourishment, and so forth, or whatever else is desired—one who accomplishes it through the yoga of passion for the wheel succeeds swiftly. (377)
As it has been said: "All the Vajra Lords, who contemplate the meaning of the reality of passion, bring about the awakening born of passion, which seeks the welfare of all sentient beings. (378)
Therefore, the practitioner seeking awakening should perform all physical, vocal, and mental activities according to the prescribed rule; all such action is intended for that very awakening. (379)
Just as for the disciples who have entered [the mandala] and desire the benefits, one should likewise grant the consolation of the three pledges according to the ritual procedure. (380)
Having seen and entered this supreme, most secret, and excellent maṇḍala,
you are today completely liberated from all sins and are well-established.
There is no further death for you from this Great Bliss Vehicle;
invincible and unbound, rejoice, free from fear from any quarter. (382)
The suffering of existence has been stilled for you, so that there may be ultimate purity from existence;
you have become the foremost among teachers for the sake of achieving the ultimate end of existence. (383)
This perfected commitment of the pledge is to be constantly guarded by you;
it is the supreme and eternal command proclaimed by all the Buddhas. (384)
The bodhicitta must certainly not be abandoned, for it is the seal known as vajra;
by its mere generation, one is indeed a Buddha—of this there is no doubt. (385)
The true Dharma must never be rejected nor ever abandoned;
