yet, out of ignorance or delusion, one should certainly not explain it [in a distorted way]. (386)
One should not afflict oneself with austerities by abandoning one's own self;
this future Buddha should be maintained in comfort according to what is pleasant. (387)
The vajra, the bell, and the mudrā must never be abandoned;
for the ācārya is not to be disparaged, as he is equal to all the Buddhas. ||388||
Slain by fevers, poisons, toxins, diseases, the afflictions of ḍākinīs, planetary influences, obstacles, and terrible Vināyakas, he shall go to hell. (390)
Therefore, with every effort, one should never at any time despise the Vajrācārya, the great guru, who is a hidden and excellent jewel. ||391||
And you should give what is appropriate, accompanied by devotion to the guru and a ritual fee (dakṣiṇā);
for thereafter, fevers and other afflictions will no longer prevail. (392)
One's own commitment must be fulfilled constantly; likewise, the Tathāgatas must be worshipped constantly;
and one must constantly give to the guru, for he is equal to all the Buddhas. (393)
From that gift comes the accumulation of merit; from the accumulation comes supreme enlightenment. What is given to him is as if given eternally to all the Buddhas. (394)
Today your birth has become fruitful, since you are well-established here;
you will become equal to the gods of the sacred times, of this there is no doubt. (395)
Today, O long-lived ones, you have been consecrated by all the Buddhas together with the Vajra-holders;
you are the firm sovereign lords of the great kingdom of the three realms. (396)
Having conquered the Māras today, you have entered the supreme city;
Buddhahood has been attained by you this very day—of this there is no doubt. (397)
Thus, fashion the diamond of a serene mind; practice your own samaya, which bestows inexhaustible bliss.
Today, in this world of fleeting happiness, [rely upon] Vajrasattva—
You have attained a state that is peerless and eternal.
Having prostrated at the feet of the guru, the disciples, who are devoted and affectionate toward the virtuous, should say: "O Lord, we shall indeed do exactly as you command. (399)
If it is possible, one should perform the rite of pacification according to the prescribed rule, grasping each of them individually with the left hand by their right thumb.
Having offered either twenty-one oblations or a single one for the sake of the king or the sovereign,
and for the pacification of the world-protectors and his own self, he should request the sacrificial fee.

In performing what is to be done for the sake of all sentient beings, or in each instance of learning and so forth, or in the attainment of one's own goals regarding land, elephants, gold, and the like, [one should provide] assistance. (402)
Having gathered those who were dismissed after being satisfied and given sacrificial fees,
one should worship the Wheel with all those means of sustenance and recreation, both one's own and those of others.

Having gathered worthy and excellent disciples, and having satisfied them with various supreme [teachings], he withdrew [the emanation] by means of the three-syllable mantras ending in the syllable *muḥ*.

Having given a small amount of powder to the petitioner with the mantra beginning with "A-kāra," one should create a great cloud of powder over the water, which is described as the supreme wheel of emptiness.

"The Master alone shall receive all that wealth which is acquired during the filling of the pit, the consecration, the fire-offering, and the ritual circle; so said the Holder of the Excellent Vajra. (406)
Thus, this clear procedure for the wheel has been taught for the beginner;
having well-attained the penetration of gnosis, it is described by means of the penetration of the being itself. (407)
Having initiated and fully worshipped a boy and a girl at the age of twelve, one should perform with them whatever ritual wheel (cakra) is intended for the mind, speech, and body. 408.
The introduction of Akṣobhya and Māmakī is proclaimed to be in the mind;
that of Pāṇḍarā and Amitābha in speech; and that of Śāśvata and Locanā in the body. (409)
This arrangement is indeed marvelous, arising from the stabilization of mind, speech, and body:
from the stabilization of the mind comes thorough knowledge, and from the stabilization of speech comes the recitation of mantras. (410)
From the paralysis of the body, there is abiding in the sky; this is the procedure for the descent of paralysis.
Here, the consecration of the teacher and the disciple is established according to the previously stated rule.
One who has attained mastery over gnosis should, by means of the mind alone, perform the triple wheel;
for through its empowerment, the wheel is perceived by both oneself and others. (412)
Entry here is permitted and is said to be like a clear dream;
therefore, it should be known as supreme because of the firmness of the mental state (*cittavṛtti*). (413)
For the three yogins as well, the procedure for the wheels of speech and body is as before;
in their place, the symbol of Akṣobhya should be present for the purification of the secrets of speech and body. (414)

Even for those who possess knowledge, those engaged in ritual action, those with defilements, those who have attained [realization], and those who have mastery, every procedure is performed by the mind alone; without that, nothing at all is accomplished.

For the foremost disciples of the Vajrācārya, whose very nature delights in the [four] results beginning with the natural outflow (niṣyanda), the procedure prescribed mentally is supreme; what would be achieved here by mere words? (416)
Buddhahood does not arise from mere conduct, nor does it come from mere learning;
it is not attained through reflection alone, but is brought to cessation through meditative cultivation. //417//
As it has been said:
"Enough with this overly prolix discourse for those who speak of mantras; the mind is what must be mastered, for from the mind arises perfect awakening. (418)
As it has been said:
"That fruit which is the thought of awakening (bodhicitta) is the unsurpassed gnosis of the Buddha;
consisting of Vajrasattva, it is the emanation of the Dharma and Enjoyment [bodies]. (419)
Since suffering consisting of cyclic existence does not arise apart from the conceptualization of the ordinary, the mind whose nature is wisdom and skillful means is the direct antidote to it. (420)
[The Ritual for the Maṇḍala of the Guhyasamāja composed by Ācārya Dīpaṃkarabhadra is completed.]
